query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloy is derived from equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi and is intended to retain a favorable strength–ductility balance in its solidified solid-solution state, but its dynamic behavior across different temperatures and strain rates lacks a theoretical explanation. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could account for this behavior, and what controlled comparison within that regime would distinguish it? Specify predictions relative to a baseline, applicable boundaries, supporting evidence, and a falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: The Co-free FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloy’s favorable strength–ductility balance is governed by a dynamic transition between dislocation glide and deformation twinning. Under certain temperature and strain‐rate conditions, local short-range ordering lowers the stacking fault energy, thereby promoting deformation twinning that both impedes dislocation motion and enhances work hardening.
generation.material_initial_state: Solid-solution state of the Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy derived from the equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi (Cantor) family
generation.intervention: Perform uniaxial mechanical tests (e.g., tensile or compression) over a controlled range of temperatures (from cryogenic to elevated temperatures) and strain rates (from quasi-static to dynamic loading conditions)
generation.conditions: Tests conducted in the solid-solution regime (i.e., avoiding conditions that trigger phase transformation or melting), across a temperature window from near cryogenic up to room/elevated temperatures and under varied strain rates
generation.structural_mediator: Strain-induced modifications in local short-range order that reduce the effective stacking fault energy, thereby facilitating the nucleation of deformation twins
generation.mechanism: At lower temperatures and/or higher strain rates, the imposed deformation promotes transient, localized atomic rearrangements (short-range ordering). This rearrangement lowers the stacking fault energy, shifting the deformation mechanism from pure dislocation slip toward an increased contribution from deformation twinning. The twins act as barriers to dislocation movement, ensuring that high strength is maintained while the additional accommodation modes provided by twinning contribute to ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to a baseline condition (room-temperature quasi-static loading), testing at lower temperatures or higher strain rates should show a measurable increase in twin density and altered dislocation patterns, leading to higher yield strength without a proportional loss in ductility.
generation.baseline: Mechanical behavior measured at room temperature under quasi-static loading conditions
generation.boundary: This mechanistic effect is expected only in the solid-solution state and within a temperature/strain rate window that does not introduce phase transitions or significant thermal softening (e.g., extremes that cause adiabatic heating or melting may mask the effect)
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative influence of strain-induced short-range ordering on stacking fault energy and twin nucleation remains to be precisely measured at the atomic scale; further characterization is needed to fully map this transition.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform in situ high-resolution TEM or SEM mechanical tests on Co-free FeNiCrMn samples while varying temperature and strain rate. Simultaneously, use atom probe tomography or diffraction-based methods to assess local short-range order and stacking fault energy indicators. Compare the deformation microstructure (i.e., twin and dislocation densities) under different loading conditions.
measurements: Yield strength and work hardening rate
Ductility metrics (e.g., total strain to failure)
Local chemical order parameters (from atom probe or diffraction)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If under low-temperature or high strain-rate conditions the alloy does not exhibit a significant increase in deformation twin density or show associated changes in local short-range order relative to the baseline—and if mechanical properties remain unchanged or do not align with the predicted shift in deformation behavior—the hypothesis is falsified.

High entropy alloys (HEAs) are a new class of metallic materials composed of multiple principle elements in equal or near-equal atomic proportions [1] , [2] . They have been receiving significant research interest owing to their exceptional mechanical and functional properties; see, e.g., refs [3] – [5] . Among various reported HEAs, the equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi (Cantor alloy) [6] is a popular and important prototype of HEAs based on 3d transition metals. Within a wide range of temperature below its solidus, it usually forms a chemically disordered solid solution in face-centered cubic (fcc) structure at ambient pressure [6] – [9] . A unique mechanical characteristic of the Cantor alloy is an enhanced strength-ductility combination with decreasing temperature, while maintaining outstanding fracture toughness at cryogenic temperatures, which was demonstrated to be closely related to the formation of nano-twins and stacking faults in deformation [7] , [10] – [15] . Furthermore, due to the irreversible pressure-induced phase transition from the fcc to the hexagonal close-packed (hcp) lattice, the presence of the hcp structure was recently observed at ambient conditions [16] – [18] .
